newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian court to rule on house arrest for ex-Nazi.
newsitem.headline: Italian court to rule on house arrest for ex-Nazi.

text.p: A military court was expected to decide on Tuesday whether to release former SS captain Erich Priebke into house arrest pending a re-trial for his part in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, his lawyer said.
Attorney Carlo Taormina said his petition to the court in Rome to ease the 83-year-old German's terms of detention on health grounds had not been opposed by the military prosecutor.
"It's looking good," Taormina told Reuters. He said the Rome military court had met on Monday. "It has already decided. Today it will announce its decision."
Court officials said the judges would convene from three p.m. (1400 GMT).
Priebke has been in jail since November 1995 when he was extradited from Argentina where he had lived openly since 1948.
He is accused of complicity in multiple murder for his role in the SS massacre of 335 men and boys at the Ardeatine Caves near Rome on March 24, 1944. Seventy-five victims were Jews.

Taormina said he had requested Priebke's release from the military jail where he is awaiting a re-trial in the case, expected to start next month, because of deteriorating mental health. Medical reports pointed to a loss of mental powers because of isolation and Priebke's advancing age, he said.
Military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano was not immediately available for comment.
Taormina declined to say where Priebke would go if released from jail but judicial sources have said he could be accommodated by a Roman Catholic Church organisation.
A military court in Naples also met on Tuesday to consider whether the arrest warrant issued after Priebke's first trial, which ended in uproar last August, was still valid.
It ruled that the detention order should not be revoked.
Priebke has admitted shooting two victims of the Caves massacre and ticking names off a list but said he had to follow orders or he would have been shot himself.
A military court found Priebke guilty last August 1 at the end of his first trial, but freed him citing extenuating circumstances which triggered a statute of limitations.
Priebke was rearrested that night after relatives of the massacre victims and other protesters laid siege to the courthouse. The verdict was quashed on appeal in October.

Another ex-Nazi, former SS major Karl Hass, is also accused of complicity in the massacre and judicial sources say the two men could be tried together. Hass, who is under house arrest, is due to go on trial on April 14.
